title: The Hospital Parking Fine
facts: At 2:10 a.m., Priya, a night-shift nurse, was called back to the hospital for an emergency.
The staff car park was full, so she left her car in a marked no-parking zone by the side entrance.
She was fined. She appealed, saying the emergency left her no choice.

parties.name: City Parking Authority
parties.wants: rules enforced the same way for everyone

evidence.label: Hospital call log
evidence.text: Shows Priya was paged at 2:04 a.m. and logged in at 2:19 a.m.

evidence.label: Camera timestamps
evidence.text: Her car was in the zone from 2:11 to 5:40 a.m.

evidence.label: A neighbour’s remark
evidence.text: “She parks there most nights.” The neighbour has never worked a shift with her.

rules: Parking in a marked no-parking zone carries a fine.
The Authority may cancel a fine if the driver proves a genuine emergency.

tree.label: Fine upheld
tree.detail: You apply the rule exactly as written.

children.label: Priya pays the fine
children.detail: She pays, and feels punished for doing her job.

children.label: Staff stop answering night calls from home
children.detail: Some staff decide a possible fine isn’t worth the risk.

children.label: Emergency response slows
children.detail: Fewer staff reach the hospital quickly at night.

children.label: The rule is seen to apply to everyone
Fewer false emergency claims
children.detail: Honest and dishonest drivers alike expect no exceptions.

children.label: Priya keeps her money and her trust in the process
children.detail: She sees the system recognise her situation.

children.label: Staff feel backed when they answer emergencies
children.detail: Word spreads that genuine emergencies are protected.

children.label: Emergency response stays fast
children.detail: Staff keep coming in without fear of a fine.

children.label: Genuine cases face long paperwork
children.detail: Honest drivers pay the price of the abuse.

reasons.text: The rule must apply equally to everyone
reasons.assumption: Exceptions will be uneven or abused.
reasons.failsWhen: Enforcing the rule defeats the reason it exists.
reasons.objection: Treating unequal situations equally can itself be unfair.
reasons.echo: Many legal systems still excuse a breach in a genuine emergency, an idea called necessity.
reasons.alternative: An outcomes-minded judge would ask what the fine actually achieves here.

reasons.text: What happens next matters more than the wording
reasons.assumption: We can predict the effects reasonably well.
reasons.failsWhen: The predictions are guesses, or the effects fall on people not in the room.
reasons.objection: Judges who chase outcomes become unpredictable, so people cannot plan around the law.
reasons.echo: Public-health rulings often weigh wider effects over strict procedure.
reasons.alternative: A rule-based judge would hold the line so everyone knows where they stand.

reasons.text: The proof must meet the exception’s test
reasons.assumption: The records are accurate and complete.
reasons.failsWhen: Records are missing, faked, or measure the wrong thing.
reasons.objection: Demanding strong proof burdens people who act honestly in a crisis.
reasons.echo: Courts routinely set different burdens of proof for different questions.
reasons.alternative: A protective judge would give the benefit of the doubt to someone acting for others.

reasons.text: Protect the people who depend on the service
reasons.assumption: Those who depend on the service are the most at risk.
reasons.failsWhen: Protecting one group quietly shifts costs onto another.
reasons.objection: It can justify bending rules whenever a sympathetic story is told.
reasons.echo: Fire and ambulance services are often given legal exemptions for this reason.
reasons.alternative: A rule-based judge would say a clear exemption belongs in the rule, not in case-by-case mercy.
